prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Ay, gaze upon her rose-wreathed hair, And gaze upon her smile; Seem as you drank the very air Her breath perfumed the while: And wake for her the gifted line, That wild and witching lay, And swear your heart is as a shrine, That only owns her sway. ’Tis well: I am revenged at last,— Mark you that scornful cheek,— The eye averted as you pass’d, Spoke more than words could speak. Ay, now by all the bitter tears That I have shed for thee,— The racking doubts, the burning fears,— Avenged they well may be— By the nights pass’d in sleepless care, The days of endless woe; All that you taught my heart to bear, All that yourself will know. I would not wish to see you laid Within an early tomb; I should forget how you betray’d, And only weep your doom: But this is fitting punishment, To live and love in vain,— Oh my wrung heart, be thou content, And feed upon his pain. Go thou and watch her lightest sigh,— Thine own it will not be; And bask beneath her sunny eye,— It will not turn on thee. ’Tis well: the rack, the chain, the wheel, Far better hadst thou proved; Ev’n I could almost pity feel, For thou art not beloved.

outputs.L1:
Here is a polished rendering of your poem, preserving its meter, rhyme scheme, and archaic diction while refining certain phrasings for greater eloquence and clarity:

---

Ay, gaze upon her rose-crowned hair,
And gaze upon her smile;
Breathe deep, as though the very air
Were sweetened by her, the while:
And summon forth the gifted line,
That wild, beguiling lay,
And vow your heart is as a shrine
Where only she holds sway.

'Tis well: my vengeance now is won,—
Behold that scornful cheek,—
The eyes that turned as you passed on
Spoke more than words could speak.

Ay, now by every bitter tear
I once shed but for thee,—
By racking doubt and burning fear,—
Avenged full well may be—
By nights consumed in sleepless care,
By days of endless woe;
All that you taught my heart to bear,
All that yourself shall know.

I would not wish to see you laid
Too soon within the tomb;
I'd then forget how you betrayed,
And only mourn your doom:
But this shall be your rightful pain—
To live, to love in vain,—
Oh, wounded heart, take thou thy fill,
And feast upon his pain.

Go, watch for her the faintest sigh,—
It shall not fall for thee;
And bask beneath her radiant eye,—
It shall not turn to thee.
'Tis well: the rack, the chain, the wheel
Had been the kinder fate;
Even I might pity feel,
For thou art loved too late.

---

outputs.L3:
# The Bitter Sweetness of Revenge

I watched him yesterday, standing beneath the garden arbor, gazing upon her with eyes full of tender devotion. She wore roses woven through her dark hair, and when she smiled at him, he seemed to lose himself entirely in that expression, as though the sun itself had condescended to shine solely for him. I have heard that he spends his evenings now composing verses in her honor, pouring out his heart in careful stanzas, offering her the kind of worship that once—though it feels like a lifetime ago—he offered to me.

Yet as I stood in the shadows and observed this tableau of devotion, an unexpected feeling crept through me: not sorrow, not even indifference, but something sharper and more satisfying. For I had witnessed, only moments before, how she received him—with a scornful curl of her lip and eyes that refused to meet his own. He passed by her afterward with his cheek burning in humiliation, his gaze fixed upon the ground, unable to look up and face what he had become in her eyes: unwanted, unworthy, unloved.

I will not pretend that I have forgotten what he did to me. The bitter tears I shed in solitude, the nights I lay awake counting the hours while doubt gnawed at my composure, the burning fears that plagued me as I wondered what I had done to deserve such careless abandonment—all of this remains etched into my memory, a wound that time has scarred but never fully healed. He was the author of that suffering, the architect of those sleepless nights, and I have carried the weight of his betrayal long after he ceased to think of me at all.

I do not wish him dead. I harbor no desire to see him suffer some violent or tragic end. But there is a certain justice, I confess, in watching him now taste the very medicine he once forced upon me. To live and love in vain—to pour out one's heart and have it returned empty, to offer devotion and receive only rejection—this is a fate that feels fitting, almost poetic in its symmetry. I will not deny that I find a bitter satisfaction in his unrequited pain, though I know such feelings reflect no particular virtue in my own character.

For what punishment could be more exquisite than this? The rack might tear the body, the chain might bind the limbs, the wheel might break the bones—but none of these instruments of torture can rival the particular anguish of loving someone who looks at you with contempt, of offering your whole heart only to have it handed back, unwanted and unclaimed. He now understands, in the deepest chambers of his being, precisely what he once inflicted upon me. And though I claim no joy in cruelty, I cannot pretend that watching him suffer this exact torment—unloved, unwanted, invisible to the very woman he adores—brings me anything but a quiet, satisfied peace.

# The Wound That Speaks

I remember when your eyes held only me,
when every word you spoke was honeyed truth,
when I believed the promises so freely
given in the reckless heat of youth.

Now I watch you chase another's shadow,
begging for the love you once discarded,
offering the same words, worn and hollow,
to a heart that leaves you always guarded.

There is something bitter in this justice—
watching you become what I once was,
pleading for a warmth that will not touch this
distance she maintains without a pause.

I confess I feel a dark contentment
seeing you consumed by what you caused,
this reflection of my own resentment
mirrored in the ache that gives you pause.

She turns from you as you once turned from me,
indifferent to the fire in your chest,
and I who bore that same disloyalty
find some comfort watching you unblessed.

Is this not the balance love requires?
That the one who wounds should feel the wound?
That the one who lit and left the fires
should burn within flames he once consumed?

Yet even as I count this fitting sentence,
even as I tally your despair,
something stirs beneath my cold repentance—
pity, unexpected, rising there.

For I know too well this desperate hunger,
this reaching for a hand that will not hold,
and though you caused a pain I bear still longer,
I would not wish this suffering, too bold.

So I stand between vindication's pleasure
and the ancient ache of shared humanity,
watching you seek what you once cast as treasure
then discarded with such vain vanity.

Perhaps this is love's final revelation—
that even in betrayal's aftermath,
we cannot fully sever the relation
that once made two hearts walk a single path.

You suffer now as I once suffered, truly,
unloved and reaching for a fading light,
and though you earned this ache so unruly,
I pity you, alone in your long night.
outputs.L5:
# Reflections on Perception

Things are rarely as they seem. We construct our understanding of the world through fragments—glimpses, impressions, half-formed thoughts—and from these pieces we assemble a picture that feels complete, even when it isn't.

Consider how we come to know another person. We meet her in passing, perhaps at a gathering where the light is dim and conversation brief. And from this single encounter, we begin to form judgments. She seems confident. She seems distracted. She seems kind, or guarded, or tired. These impressions feel immediate and true, yet they are built on so little.

And this is the strange alchemy of human perception: we take fragments and mistake them for wholes. Her laugh in that one moment becomes, in our minds, evidence of her entire disposition. The way she seemed to hesitate before answering a question becomes proof of some deeper uncertainty in her character.

But seeming is not being. What appears true in a glance may unravel entirely upon closer acquaintance. The woman who seemed aloof at the party might simply have been nervous, overwhelmed by unfamiliar faces. And the confidence we read into her posture might have been armor, not ease.

This gap between appearance and reality is not a flaw to be corrected but a condition to be recognized. We can never fully know another person—not truly, not completely. We only ever encounter fragments: how someone seems in this moment, under these circumstances, filtered through our own expectations and biases.

And perhaps this is why patience matters so much in how we come to understand others. Her first impression is never her final truth. Neither is our first impression of her.

The wisest approach, then, may be to hold our judgments loosely—to notice how someone seems while remaining open to discovering how she actually is.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a Victorian-style poem about a woman watching her former lover pursue someone else, feeling both heartbreak and vengeful satisfaction.
counterfactuals.output:
**At the Assembly**

I watch him bend to whisper low
Against another's waiting ear—
The very words, so soft, so slow,
He once did murmur in my ear.

Her fan doth flutter at his jest,
Her cheek doth bloom a rosy shade;
I know that warmth within her breast—
I know how soon such warmth doth fade.

O heart, be still, though torn and bruised,
Though every glance a dagger seems;
He loved me once, and then he used
The self-same tongue for softer schemes.

Yet there's a bitter, secret glee
That stirs beneath my grief's dark tide—
For she who wears his gaze shall see
What I have learned, and learned, and cried.

She does not know the hollow art
Of pretty vows too lightly made,
Nor how a false and fickle heart
Can smile, and charm, and then evade.

I pity her, yet still rejoice—
Is that not strange, that I should feel
Both sorrow's ache and vengeance' voice
Twined tight as thread upon a wheel?

For love once given, cruelly spent,
Doth leave the spirit halved in two:
One half in mourning, sore, unspent—
One half that whispers, *"Now she'll rue."*

So let the candles gild his face,
So let her laugh at all he'll say—
I'll wear my grief with quiet grace,
And wait, and watch, and walk away.

For time, that patient, silent guest,
Doth strip the mask from every lover's guile;
And she will learn, as I have learned—
Behind his charm, a colder smile.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dramatic 19th-century-style poem in rhyming quatrains about betrayed love and bittersweet revenge, using archaic language like "thee," "thou," and "hadst."
counterfactuals.output:
**The Serpent in the Garden of My Heart**

Thou cam'st to me in springtime's golden hour,
When blossoms wept their petals at thy feet,
And I, poor fool, did worship at thy bower,
Believing every honeyed word too sweet.

I gave thee all—my soul, my nights, my days,
Hadst thou but asked, I'd giv'n my very breath.
Yet thou didst trade my love for fleeting praise,
And left my trusting heart to waste toward death.

I saw thee then, beneath the willow's shade,
Entwined with one whose name I shall not speak—
Thy vows to me like autumn leaves did fade,
While laughter mocked the tears upon my cheek.

Oh, wherefore didst thou break what was so true?
What cruel design didst move thy faithless breast?
I loved thee more than morning loves the dew,
Yet thou didst cast my devotion like a jest.

So I did wait, as patient as the grave,
And watched thy new-found joy begin to wane,
For love that's built on falsehood cannot save
A heart from reaping what deceit hath sown.

I did not curse thee, nor did I destroy—
I simply let thee drown in thine own lies.
Thy paramour soon wearied of her toy,
And left thee weeping 'neath these very skies.

Now thou dost wander, hollow-eyed and lone,
Where once thou reigned with careless, cruel delight,
While I stand here, mine anguish turned to stone,
Watching thy sorrow bloom into the night.

'Tis bittersweet, this vengeance I did reap—
No joy have I in thy belated pain,
Yet still I cannot help but softly weep
For love that's lost and never comes again.

For though thou'rt broken as I once did break,
And though the scales of justice now stand true,
I'd trade this hollow triumph, for thy sake,
To have again the love I thought I knew.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a poem in the voice of a scorned woman who takes grim comfort in knowing her ex-lover will never be loved as she loved him?
counterfactuals.output:
# What You'll Never Have Again

I hope she's kind. I do. I hope
she brings you soup when you are sick,
and doesn't count the days you owe her,
and laughs at jokes you tell too quick.

I hope she's patient with your silence,
the way you disappear mid-thought.
I hope she never has to wonder
what storm you're weathering, uncaught.

But I was there before the quiet
learned to live inside your chest.
I mapped the weather of your leaving
before you knew it as unrest.

No one will study you like scripture,
the way I did, in candlelight—
each scar a verse I memorized,
each silence a hymn I got right.

She'll love you well. I don't doubt that.
Some easier, lighter kind of love—
the kind that doesn't ask the questions
I bled myself to answer, above

and past what should have broken me.
She'll never know that particular ache
of loving someone past the limit,
past reason, past your own mistake.

And that's the thing you'll carry always,
some hollow that she'll never fill—
because I loved you like a fever,
and fevers break, but leave a chill

that lesser warmths can't quite reach.
So love her softly. Love her true.
But you'll feel me in every winter,
the cold shape of what I gave to you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a Romantic-era poem exploring themes of jealousy, unrequited love, and quiet vengeance, written in formal, elevated diction similar to Byron or Tennyson.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Serpent's Patience**

I loved thee once with such a flame
As lights the martyr to his pyre—
Yet thou didst wear another's name
Upon thy lips, and called it fire.

I saw thee smile on him whose eyes
Held nothing of the soul's deep well;
I watched thee weave beneath fair skies
A tapestry I dared not tell.

Oh, jealousy! Thou subtle thief,
That steals the peace from out the breast,
And leaves behind but silent grief
Dressed in the guise of patient rest—

I did not rage, I did not weep
Before the world's unfeeling eye;
I let the wound go still and deep,
And learned the art to seem, not sigh.

For vengeance wears no crimson glove,
No dagger gleaming in the night—
She comes as memory of love
Grown cold within another's sight.

I'll be the ghost within thy hall,
The whisper in thy husband's ear,
The shadow lengthening on the wall
When autumn strips the dying year.

Thou'lt see my face in every glass,
Reflected in each fading rose,
And know, too late, what thou didst pass—
The heart that time can not depose.

So let the years like rivers run,
And let thy laughter fill the hall;
I am the setting of thy sun,
The quiet architect of all.

For love refused becomes a seed
That roots itself in patient soil,
And blooms, at last, a darker weed
Watered by another's toil.

Sleep well, fair scorner of my heart—
I hold no blade, I speak no curse.
I simply wait, a work of art
Unfinished, growing worse and worse
Within thy dreams, where I shall dwell
Long after love has said farewell.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem where the speaker addresses her former love directly, describing his new romance while reflecting on her own suffering and finding solace in his inevitable emotional punishment.
counterfactuals.output:
# What I Hear of You

I hear she laughs the way you like—
too loud, then quick to cover her mouth,
as if she's still deciding who she's allowed to be
around you. I remember that stage.
It doesn't last.

You'll teach her, without meaning to,
how to read the weather of your silences,
how a closed door means something different
than it says. She'll learn to translate you
the way I did—badly, hopefully,
then well, then too well.

I don't say this to wish her harm.
I say it because I know the shape
of what's coming, the way you'll turn
warm one day and distant the next,
and call it constancy. The way you'll need
without asking, and be wounded
when the need goes unmet, as if
you hadn't hidden it like a blade
in your sleeve.

I spent two years learning your weather.
I got good at bracing before the storm
that never announced itself,
only arrived, then left, then blamed the leaving
on the wind.

So no—I don't wish her harm.
I wish her something worse, and kinder:
I wish her the full length of you,
the whole slow unfolding,
until she stands where I stand now,
not broken, exactly, but instructed—
fluent in a language
she never should have had to learn.

You'll feel it, eventually.
Not because I curse you.
Because it's you. Because this is simply
what you do to people
who let themselves be loved by you,
and what, in time,
gets done to you as well.

I don't need to raise my voice.
I just need to wait.
The same patience you taught me
will teach you something, too—
how it feels to reach
for a door that isn't there,
to learn, too late,
what weather you had made.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
